title: The Contact Center Agent Retention Playbook
subtitle: How to stop rehiring your frontline every year, in-house or outsourced
audience: For CX and contact center executives, COOs, CFOs, workforce leaders and BPO leaders.
byline: Brett Kiley, Founder and CEO, Experience Improvement Partners | October 2026

blocks.text: Executive summary

runs.t: Contact centers have normalized something no other part of the business would accept: replacing about three in ten frontline people every year. At outsourcing partners, it is often much higher. AI is now taking the easy contacts, which leaves agents with the hardest ones. Retention has never mattered more, or been managed less.
1. Attrition is stuck.
Mean U.S. agent attrition has run at 29% to 31% from 2023 to 2025, and in the 2023 data a fifth of centers were above 50%.
2. New agents leave fastest, and it is getting worse.
22% of U.S. centers now lose more than a quarter of new agents within 90 days, up from 12% two survey waves earlier.
3. Outsourced turnover is a different scale.
One of the largest global BPOs reported 67.6% agent attrition in 2024 and hired 389,220 people to keep headcount flat.
4. The job design drives it.
Turnover runs 9% where agents have discretion and light monitoring, and 36% where they have little discretion and heavy monitoring.
5. The contract rarely pays for retention.
Most outsourcing is priced per hour, per minute or per agent. At one major BPO, performance bonuses and penalties are under 1% of revenue.
Our view:

for contact centers, retention is a customer experience strategy. Every agent you keep past six months is an agent who can handle the hard contacts AI leaves behind. Every agent you lose in training is money spent on someone who never helped a customer.

blocks.text: The state of the agent workforce
Attrition is stuck around 30%

runs.t: ContactBabel's 2026 U.S. Contact Center Decision-Makers' Guide surveyed 207 U.S. contact center leaders. Mean annual agent attrition was 29% in 2025, 30% in 2024 and 31% in 2023. Medians run lower, which means a group of centers with very high attrition pulls the average up. In the 2023 data, a quarter of centers were at 10% or less, while 21% were above 50%. The difference between those two groups is mostly how they run the work.

blocks.title: “Attrition in the US right now is about 30% on average, and that's been pretty standard for the past seven or eight years.”
lines: Steve Morrell, Managing Director, ContactBabel. No Jitter, April 2026.

blocks.text: New agents leave before they are worth the investment

runs.t: The first 90 days are where most of the money is lost. In 2025, 22% of U.S. centers lost more than a quarter of new agents within three months. It takes six months or more for a new agent to perform like an experienced one. An agent who leaves in month two has cost you recruiting, weeks of paid training and nesting, and never reached full speed.

blocks.text: Outsourced turnover runs at a different scale

items.label: annual agent attrition at Teleperformance in 2024 (global)
hires to keep headcount flat at about 489,000
average turnover at U.S. outsourced centers (Cornell)

runs.t: Teleperformance, one of the largest outsourcing companies in the world, reported average agent attrition of 5.6% a month in 2024, or 67.6% for the year. To stay the same size, it hired 389,220 people. Cornell's national U.S. study found outsourced centers averaged 51% turnover, against 33% overall. If you outsource, the attrition you pay for is often hidden inside your vendor's price.

blocks.text: Agents can earn more down the road

runs.t: The median U.S. customer service representative earns $21.53 an hour. At outsourcing companies, the median is $17.68. Warehouse laborers in warehousing earn a median of $22.06, and Amazon says its fulfillment and transportation workers average more than $23 an hour. Contact centers with lower early attrition pay new agents about 10% more than those with high early attrition, according to ContactBabel. Pay matters. But the research below shows that how the job feels matters as much.

blocks.text: What industry leaders are saying

blocks.title: “They don't want to be sitting there doing mindless, repetitive tasks over and over.”
lines: Anna Convery, Chief Marketing Officer, Verint, on what agents want. No Jitter, April 2026.

blocks.title: “...pushed agents into a perpetual 'escalation' role, which many agents report is draining and stressful.”
lines: Riccardo Pasto, Principal Analyst, Forrester Research, on how AI is changing the agent job. destinationCRM, January 2026.

blocks.title: “Customer service and support leaders should avoid framing AI initiatives solely around headcount reduction.”
lines: Melissa Fletcher, Senior Principal, Research, Gartner. December 2025.

blocks.text: Our assessment: why agents really leave

runs.t: Contact center leaders rank "wrong type of person for the job" and low pay as the top reasons agents leave. Agents themselves point to unrealistic performance expectations (47%) and no schedule flexibility (45%), according to Verint's 2026 survey of 1,000 agents. In our experience, these six forces explain most of it.
1. The job is designed like an assembly line.
Scripts, handle-time targets and constant monitoring leave no room for judgment. The research is clear: where agents have discretion, turnover drops by three quarters.
2. The schedule belongs to someone else.
Adherence rules and fixed shifts collide with childcare, school and second jobs. Schedule flexibility is one of the top reasons agents choose, or leave, a job.
3. AI took the easy calls.
What is left is harder, longer and more emotional. Calls today are about 80% longer than in 2003, and managers now rank empathy as the most valued agent trait.
4. Hiring fills seats, not roles.
When the goal is a headcount number by a date, the process selects people who can start, not people who will stay.
5. The supervisor has too many people and too little time.
Coaching gets squeezed by reporting and escalations. Agents get feedback only when a metric is red.
6. The contract pays for time.
When an outsourcing partner is paid per hour or per agent, losing and replacing agents can cost the client more than it costs the vendor.

The job design evidence is old but consistent. The Global Call Center Report, covering about 2,500 centers in 17 countries, found 9% turnover where agents had high discretion and light monitoring, against 36% where they had low discretion and heavy monitoring. Cornell's U.S. study found production-line centers averaged 45% turnover, against 25% for high-involvement centers.

blocks.text: What we saw: 2,000 hires, and paying for bodies

runs.t: Before founding EIP, I spent 20 years in operations and patient experience at a Fortune 10 company. In one business, I led patient experience strategy across a contact center operation of about 7,500 agents: about 4,000 of our own employees and 3,500 from outsourcing partners.

Every year we hired about 2,000 people between August and December to be trained and taking calls on January 1. 42% of them never made it to that first day. After we redesigned how we hired, with a shorter process and new screening built around the people who stayed, that fell to 15%. That was about 540 more trained agents in a seat on day one.

Our outsourcing partners told us their turnover averaged about 30% a month. Then we looked at the contract. We paid them for having enough people in seats on January 1, not for whether those people were good or whether they stayed. We changed the incentive and the payment plan, and their turnover dropped significantly.

Over the same two years, by improving the employee experience and the customer experience together, our Net Promoter Score went from 24 to 81, and the solutions we delivered added $104 million in operating profit.
The lesson:
whatever you pay for is what you get. Pay for bodies by a date and you will get bodies by a date. Pay for people who stay and serve customers well, and you will get them.

blocks.text: AI changes the job. It can also keep your people

runs.t: The best evidence on AI and agent retention comes from a study of 5,172 agents published by Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li and Lindsey Raymond. When agents had a generative AI assistant, issues resolved per hour rose 15% on average, with the biggest gains for newer and less-skilled agents. Attrition among agents with under six months of tenure fell by about 10 points from a 25% baseline, a 40% cut. Agents with two months of tenure performed like unassisted agents with more than six. The authors caution the attrition result may be overstated.

Gartner's 2026 research shows most service leaders are not using AI to lay people off. 63% are reducing headcount gradually through attrition, and 85% are adding responsibilities to agent roles. That means fewer agents, doing harder work, who need to stay longer. AI makes retention more important, not less.

blocks.text: What an agent departure really costs

runs.t: EIP's Turn Tax™ builds the cost of turnover across 13 categories and up to 250 variables. For contact center agents, it runs about 25% to 40% of annual pay. The biggest pieces are lost productivity and customer impact, not job ads. That lines up with the Global Call Center Report, which put the full cost at three to four months of pay once lost productivity is included.

Fix the first 90 days: shorter wait to start, a peer mentor for every new agent, ramped metrics and a stable schedule.

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: CEO: Ask what share of last year's new agents were gone within 90 days. That is the cleanest single measure of whether your hiring and onboarding work.
CFO: Add recruiting, training and nesting costs for agents who left before day 90. That is money spent on people who never fully served a customer.
COO or CX leader: Pick the supervisor with the most turnover and the one with the least. Compare their team sizes and coaching time.
Workforce management: Count schedule change requests denied last month. Each one is a small reason to leave.
CHRO: Pull your outsourcing contracts. Find out what you pay for: seats, hours or results.

title: The Home Health Clinician Retention Playbook
subtitle: How to keep the nurses and therapists your agency cannot grow without
audience: For CEOs, CFOs, COOs, CHROs and Chief Clinical Officers of Medicare-certified home health agencies.
byline: Brett Kiley, Founder and CEO, Experience Improvement Partners | October 2026

items.label: annual RN turnover in home health
of home health referrals accepted in 2024
Medicare home health payment change for 2026

blocks.text: Executive summary

runs.t: Home health has more patients than it can serve and fewer clinicians than it needs. The constraint on growth is no longer referrals. It is the number of nurses and therapists who stay long enough to take a full caseload.
1. You lose about one RN in four every year.
Home health RN turnover was 25.46% in 2025, compared with 17.6% for hospital RNs.
2. Most of that loss happens early.
In one study, 34% of new full-time home health nurses and 45% of part-time nurses left in their first year, most within 180 days.
3. Unfilled seats are turning patients away.
Home health referral acceptance was 34.5% in 2024, even as referrals rose 6%. In Texas alone, 34 agencies declined 6,625 patients in a year for lack of staff.
4. You cannot pay your way out.
Medicare cut aggregate home health payments 1.3% for 2026, and MedPAC has recommended a further 7% cut to the base rate. All-payer margins for freestanding agencies were 5.0% in 2024.
5. The biggest lever is one most agencies already control: the schedule.
Full-time RNs with the most volatile schedules were 50% more likely to quit. Those with the most stable schedules were 40% less likely.
Our view:

retention in home health is a capacity strategy, not an HR program. Every clinician you keep is a caseload you can staff, a referral you can accept and a start of care you can make on time. This playbook shows where clinicians leave, what it costs, what each executive sees, and what to do in the next 90 days.

blocks.text: The state of the home health workforce
Turnover is high, and it starts early

runs.t: The Hospital and Healthcare Compensation Service surveyed 1,111 home health agencies for its 2025-2026 report. RN turnover improved slightly, from 26.95% to 25.46%, and 36.52% of agencies said turnover fell in the past year. That still means a typical agency replaces a quarter of its RNs every year, at a time when the average RN sign-on bonus has reached $7,499.
Even the largest operators feel it. Amedisys, one of the biggest home health companies in the country, reported voluntary turnover between 16.8% and 20.5% each quarter of 2024 in its SEC filings.

The first six months decide most of it. When researchers followed home health nurses at a large agency, a third of new full-time nurses and nearly half of part-time nurses were gone within a year. Voluntary departures outnumbered involuntary ones almost four to one. These are not people being let go. They are people choosing to leave.

blocks.title: What about therapists?
lines: No free national source publishes home health turnover for physical, occupational and speech therapists. The public data shows this much.
Pay is not the main gap. Home health already pays physical therapists more than hospitals do: a median of $114,740, against $106,800 (BLS, May 2025).

The work itself has changed. Therapy visits per 30-day period fell 21.5% from 2019 to 2024, from 4.9 to 3.8 (MedPAC). Fewer visits can mean less predictable caseloads and pay for therapists paid per visit.
The role mix is shifting. At Amedisys, therapy assistants made up 54.4% of therapy staff by late 2024 (SEC filings). Therapists increasingly supervise as well as treat.
Unpaid time is common. One in three home health speech-language pathologists works off the clock every day (ASHA, 2025).
The hospital baseline is lower. In hospitals, annual turnover is 10.2% for physical therapists, 9.1% for occupational therapists and 9.8% for speech-language pathologists (NSI, 2026).

Our read: for therapists, schedule and caseload stability, documentation time and a clear role next to assistants matter more than another raise. A Retention Snapshot shows exactly where your own therapists stand.

blocks.text: The money is getting tighter

runs.t: CMS finalized a 1.3% aggregate cut to Medicare home health payments for 2026, about $220 million. For 2027, CMS has proposed a 2.4% aggregate increase that still includes a 3.0% temporary cut to the rate. MedPAC voted unanimously in March 2026 to recommend Congress cut the base rate 7%. Medicare margins look healthy on paper, at 21.2% for freestanding agencies in 2024, but all-payer margins were only 5.0%.

Care is also being delivered with fewer visits. In-person visits per 30-day period fell 18% from 2019 to 2024. Therapy visits fell 21.5%. Each visit carries more weight, and each clinician you lose takes a bigger share of your capacity with them.

Outside California, the number of Medicare-certified agencies fell from 9,823 to 9,320 between 2019 and 2024. The market is consolidating. Agencies that can staff will take share from agencies that cannot.

blocks.text: Your RN competitor is the hospital

runs.t: Home health already pays therapists and LPNs more than hospitals do. The median physical therapist in home health earns $114,740, compared with $106,800 in hospitals. RNs are different. The hospital median is $100,220, and travel nurses average about $91 an hour. That is the gap your recruiters are fighting, and it is why pay alone rarely wins the retention battle for RNs.

blocks.text: What industry leaders are saying

blocks.title: “The population in need of our care is growing much faster than the clinical labor pool.”
lines: Barb Jacobsmeyer, President and CEO, Enhabit Home Health & Hospice. Home Health Care News, August 2025.

blocks.title: “[T]he industry-wide shortage of experienced RNs and field clinicians remains our most pressing challenge.”
lines: G. Scott Herman, Founder and CEO, New Day Healthcare. Home Health Care News, January 2026.

blocks.title: “Patients need the level of care that home health provides, yet the capacity to care for all of those patients is constrained.”
lines: Tim Ashe, Chief Clinical Officer, WellSky. Home Health Care News, October 2024.

blocks.title: “Nurses, therapists, and aides remain the backbone of this industry, and we must continue to invest in them.”
lines: Jonathan Fleece, President and CEO, Empath Health. Home Health Care News, January 2026.

blocks.title: “Devoting time to retention is the most efficient, economical and successful way to deal with the workforce shortages today.”
lines: Bill Dombi, Senior Counsel, Arnall Golden Gregory. Home Health Care News, September 2025.

blocks.text: Our assessment: why clinicians really leave

runs.t: Pay matters, and it gets most of the attention. In our experience, and in the research, it is rarely the first thing that pushes a clinician out the door. These are the six forces we look for first.
1. The schedule is the job.

A clinician's week is set by a scheduler they may never meet. When visit counts swing week to week, pay swings and family plans fall apart. The research is clear: schedule volatility predicts quitting more strongly than almost anything else an agency controls.
2. The first 180 days decide it.
Orientation, field shadowing and the first solo caseload are where most clinicians are lost. A new nurse who feels thrown into the car alone with a full caseload starts looking within weeks.
3. Charting is a second shift.

Documentation follows clinicians home. The 2025 ASHA survey found one in three home health speech-language pathologists works off the clock every day. Research links documentation burden and visit pressure to burnout and intent to leave.
4. The manager is in the office. The clinician is in the field.

Clinical managers often have large teams spread across long drive times. Field clinicians can go weeks without a real conversation with their manager. Isolation is built into the job unless the agency designs against it.
5. The hospital is always hiring.
RNs can usually earn more in a hospital or through travel work. You will not always win on pay. You can win on schedule, support and how it feels to work for you.
6. Every loss lands on someone else.
When one clinician leaves, the remaining team absorbs the visits. Overtime, longer days and missed visits raise everyone else's risk. Turnover spreads.
This is not a criticism of home health leaders.
Most of these forces come from how the work is built, not from bad intentions. That is good news. What is built can be rebuilt.

blocks.text: We have done this with licensed clinicians

runs.t: Before founding EIP, I spent 20 years in operations and patient experience at a Fortune 10 company. When a new competitor opened a large facility in our market, my region lost 72 of its 348 pharmacists in six months. Many took pay cuts of up to 15% to leave. We stopped guessing, asked the clinicians who stayed what would make the job workable, and fixed it. Pharmacist turnover fell from 42% to 18% within about three months of the changes, and later as low as 9%.

In another part of the company, I led patient experience strategy. Over two years, by improving the employee experience and the patient experience together, our Net Promoter Score went from 24 to 81. Licensed clinicians are not a different species. They leave for the same reasons everyone else does, and they stay for the same reasons too.

runs.t: The same turnover number looks different from every seat at the leadership table. A retention plan only works when all of them see the whole picture.

New clinicians are not ready for a solo caseload. Tenured preceptors are burning out.
Quality and documentation risk, survey and compliance exposure, and the loss of the experienced clinicians who train everyone else.

runs.t: Every clinician moves through the same six stages. Each stage has a predictable point of failure, a warning sign you can see in data you already have, and a fix.

Describe the schedule, caseload and on-call in the posting and the interview.

blocks.text: What a clinician departure really costs

runs.t: EIP's Turn Tax™ builds the cost of turnover from the ground up across 13 categories and up to 250 variables. For nurses, the cost runs from about 80% to 120% of annual salary. The largest pieces are not recruiting fees. They are safety and compliance risk, and the clinical knowledge that walks out the door.

For comparison, the 2026 NSI report puts the average cost of replacing a hospital bedside RN at $60,090, with 78 days to recruit an experienced RN. Our number also counts what happens to your patients, your referral sources and the clinicians who stay.

Stabilize the schedule. Measure week-to-week swings in visits for every full-time clinician. Set a target and hold schedulers to it.
Build the loop. Weekly manager check-ins for new clinicians, a named preceptor for every hire, and a monthly review of who needs a conversation.

title: The Nuclear Operator Retention Playbook
subtitle: How to keep the licensed and non-licensed operators your plants cannot run without
audience: For CEOs, Chief Nuclear Officers, Site Vice Presidents, CFOs and CHROs of nuclear and power generation companies.
byline: Brett Kiley, Founder and CEO, Experience Improvement Partners | October 2026

items.label: active NRC-licensed power reactor operators in the U.S.
months of site training to license one
growth in nuclear operator job postings, 2023 to 2025

blocks.text: Executive summary

runs.t: Nuclear is growing again. Plants are extending their licenses to 80 years, three shut-down plants are restarting, new reactors are being permitted and the largest technology companies are signing long-term power contracts. All of it depends on a small, hard-to-replace group of people: the operators.
1. The pool is small.
About 3,600 people hold active NRC licenses to operate U.S. power reactors.
2. Turnover is rising.
Turnover among nuclear plant operators rose from 4.1% in 2020 to 7.0% in 2022, and to 10.4% at non-fleet sites.
3. Every loss takes years to replace.
Site training to license an operator usually takes 18 to 24 months. A senior reactor operator also needs 18 months of plant experience first.
4. Everyone is hiring the same people.
Postings for nuclear power plant operators rose nearly tenfold from 2023 to 2025. More than a third of new power and data center postings target the same workers.
5. The reasons people leave are controllable.
Nuclear HR leaders name leadership, career opportunity and work-life balance or schedule changes as the top reasons for voluntary turnover.
Our view:

for a nuclear operator, retention is a license-protection strategy. Every operator you keep is a licensed seat you do not have to rebuild over two years, a shift you do not have to fill with overtime, and an outage you do not have to staff from someone else's plant.

blocks.text: The state of the operator workforce
Turnover is rising, fastest at smaller operators

runs.t: Idaho National Laboratory's 2023 study of nuclear hiring and retention found operator turnover rising every year from 2020 to 2022. Non-fleet sites, which cannot move people between plants, saw it climb fastest, to 10.4%. Across all plant employees, turnover averaged 7.3% from 2010 to 2022 and reached about 9% in 2022. Average staffing at sites fell 17.7% from 2011 to 2021. Plants are running leaner, so each departure matters more.

blocks.text: Every loss is a two-year rebuild

runs.t: The NRC exam itself is rarely the problem. Reactor operator pass rates have held between 93% and 98%. The problem is time. Site training programs usually run 18 to 24 months, and the exam takes about two weeks. Senior reactor operator candidates need 18 months of responsible plant experience before they even start. The NRC has also noted a downward trend in senior reactor operator operating-test pass rates since fiscal 2022.

Once licensed, operators keep earning that license. Requalification includes a written exam every two years and an annual operating test, and the license itself expires after six years. Some utilities describe licensed operators spending one week in five in training.

blocks.text: The minimum crew is set by law

runs.t: Federal rules set the minimum licensed staff on every shift. With one unit operating, a site needs at least two senior reactor operators and two reactor operators on shift, with a senior reactor operator in the control room at all times. You cannot run lean on licensed people. When one leaves, the gap is filled with overtime, inside limits set by the NRC's fatigue rules.

blocks.text: Demand is surging

items.label: of the U.S. fleet intends to operate for 80 years or more (NEI)
expected growth in nuclear workforce demand by 2050 (DOE)
of nuclear power in Big Tech's pipeline (NEI)

runs.t: The Department of Energy's Energy Workforce Advisory Board expects demand for the nuclear workforce to triple by 2050, and names an aging workforce, high retirement rates and a shortage of new entrants as the barriers. Idaho National Laboratory estimates about 4,000 hires a year are needed just to sustain today's fleet.

Restarts are drawing from the same small pool. The Crane Clean Energy Center, formerly Three Mile Island Unit 1, plans to hire more than 600 people. Duane Arnold is targeting about 100 licensed operators before restart. Palisades requalified 26 former licensed operators to come back.

blocks.text: Your operators are being recruited

runs.t: Deloitte's 2026 analysis of job postings found that postings for nuclear power plant operators increased nearly tenfold between 2023 and 2025. Power sector postings for core roles rose 20% while data center postings rose 64%, and more than a third of new postings targeted the same set of workers. Your operators are visible, credentialed and in demand.

Nuclear reactor operators earn a median of $122,890, well above fossil and gas plant operators. Pay matters, but every plant competing for your operators can match it. What they cannot easily copy is how it feels to work on your crews.

blocks.text: What industry leaders are saying

blocks.title: “Growth is an opportunity; but it is also creating challenges because we need more workers, both at our existing plants and the new reactor vendors.”
lines: Jeff Place, Executive Vice President for Industry Strategy, Institute of Nuclear Power Operations (INPO). ANS Nuclear Newswire, January 2026.

blocks.title: “Workforce development and supply-chain expansion are not separate challenges; they are enabling conditions for sustained deployment.”
lines: Maria Korsnick, President and CEO, Nuclear Energy Institute. Testimony to the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Energy, June 2026.

blocks.title: “The number one answer is ... 'Workforce.'”
lines: Craig Piercy, American Nuclear Society, on what keeps nuclear executives up at night. Nuclear News, August 2025.

blocks.text: Our assessment: why operators really leave

runs.t: Exit data from nuclear HR leaders points to leadership, career opportunity and schedule. Those match what we see in every licensed, shift-based workforce. These are the six forces we look for first.
1. The shift is the life.
Rotating 12-hour shifts, outage seasons and schedule changes shape everything outside work. When the rotation changes without warning, or outages stretch the crew, family life takes the hit.
2. Overtime fills every gap.
Because crew minimums are fixed, one departure becomes overtime for everyone else, right up to the fatigue limits. Turnover spreads across the crew.
3. The license is portable.
An NRC license and plant experience make an operator one of the most marketable people in energy. Restarts, new builds and data centers all know where to find them.
4. The path to senior reactor operator and shift manager is narrow.
Upgrade classes are limited. An operator passed over for the next class may decide the next step is at another site.
5. Leadership is felt on the crew.
Shift managers and operations leaders set the culture of the control room. Exit data names leadership first.
6. Training never stops.
Requalification, simulator time and one week in five in training are part of the job. Done well, it builds pride. Done poorly, it feels like being tested forever.
These are design problems, not people problems.
They come from how shifts, upgrade paths and overtime are built. What is built can be rebuilt.

blocks.text: We have done this with licensed, hard-to-replace people

runs.t: Before founding EIP, I spent 20 years in operations at a Fortune 10 company. When a new competitor opened a large facility in our market, my region lost 72 of its 348 licensed pharmacists in six months. Many took pay cuts to leave. Their license made them easy to recruit, and like your operators, they took years to develop. We asked the ones who stayed what would make the job workable, and fixed it. Pharmacist turnover fell from 42% to 18% within about three months, and later as low as 9%.

In energy, we built a Flight Risk Score for an oil and gas company from the HR data of about 600 people. When we presented it to their leadership team, every name was removed. The person at the top of the list scored 82. All we showed was his region. Someone from HR looked at the first row and asked, "Is that Daniel?" It was. "Daniel quit last week."

rows: What they see as the problem

Contracts with technology companies and capacity commitments depend on licensed people you may not have in two years.

Crew fatigue, morale and the steady loss of the experience that keeps a control room calm.
Training pipelines, retention bonuses and overtime keep growing.
Each licensed departure carries two years of training cost and lost capacity, and it rarely shows up as one line.
We cannot hire licensed operators. We have to build them.
Recruiting cannot outrun turnover when replacement takes two years. Retention is the only fast lever.

Give every operator a visible path and timeline to a license class.

blocks.text: What an operator departure really costs

runs.t: EIP's Turn Tax™ builds the cost of turnover across 13 categories and up to 250 variables. For a licensed operator, the cost runs from about 250% to 600% of annual salary. The biggest piece is the replacement's own pay: 12 to 24 months of full salary and benefits while they train and cannot stand watch. Then come the candidates who never earn a license, instructors and simulator time, and NRC exam fees. The one published industry figure, about $500,000 to train a licensed operator (Utilities Service Alliance, 2019), sits right at the middle of that range. Our range leaves out overtime, ramp-up time and lost generation, so it is conservative.

title: The Portfolio Talent Retention Playbook
subtitle: How to keep the people your value-creation plan depends on, from diligence to exit
audience: For operating partners, deal partners, human capital partners and portfolio company CEOs and CFOs.
byline: Brett Kiley, Founder and CEO, Experience Improvement Partners | October 2026

items.label: of PE deals had at least one CEO change during the hold
of PE executives say unplanned CEO turnover lengthens the hold

blocks.text: Executive summary

runs.t: Multiple expansion is no longer carrying returns. Holds are longer, exits are slower and value has to be built inside the company. That puts the people who run the operation at the center of every deal thesis. Most firms still manage that risk after it shows up.
1. Leaders turn over constantly.
69% of PE deals in a recent study had at least one CEO change during the hold. 60% of acquired companies replaced the CFO.
2. Unplanned turnover costs time and returns.
83% of PE executives say unplanned CEO turnover lengthens the hold, and nearly half say it reduces returns.
3. Timing is everything.
Companies that appointed a new CEO in year one exited after 4.4 years on average. Those that waited past year two took 7.7 years.
4. Retention bonuses only rent loyalty.
Most acquirers keep their retention agreement signers through the period. A year after it ends, far fewer do.
5. Below the CEO, the risk is mostly unmeasured.
Only 26% of portfolio companies have succession planning, and 35% have a formal employee retention program.
Our view:

in a PE-backed company, retention is a value-protection strategy. The people below the CEO carry the customer relationships, the operating know-how and the integration work that the value-creation plan assumes will happen. Knowing who is at risk before close, and in the first 100 days, is cheaper than replacing them in year two.

blocks.text: The state of portfolio talent
Leaders are replaced often, and rarely from inside

runs.t: Russell Reynolds Associates studied 196 European PE exits from 2020 to 2025. In 69% of deals, the company changed CEO at least once during the hold, and only 30% of those companies promoted an internal candidate. A separate Russell Reynolds study of about 3,000 European portfolio CFOs found 60% of companies replaced the CFO after acquisition, and only 7% of replacements were internal.

AlixPartners' 2026 PE Leadership Survey of 427 PE and portfolio company leaders found 65% of PE firms report CEO turnover during the hold, and only 9% say they rarely replace CEOs. 38% of portfolio company executives worry about losing their own jobs because of disruption.

blocks.text: Unplanned turnover stretches the hold

runs.t: When a CEO change happens matters as much as whether it happens. In the Russell Reynolds data, a new CEO appointed in year one was associated with exit after 4.4 years on average, against 7.7 years when the appointment came after year two. Each additional change pushed the average hold further, to 11.0 years with four CEO changes. This is a correlation, not proof of cause, but the direction is clear: late, unplanned leadership change costs time.

blocks.text: Below the top, turnover follows the deal

runs.t: Peer-reviewed research shows the people below the C-suite move too. In Germany, a study of more than 152,000 employees of buyout targets found lower employment and higher employee turnover after the deal. In the U.S., employment fell 12% over two years after buyouts of public companies and grew 15% after buyouts of private firms, so the effect depends heavily on the deal.

Healthcare roll-ups show it clearly. In ophthalmology practices acquired by PE from 2014 to 2021, year-to-year physician turnover was 13 percentage points, or 265%, higher than in practices that were not acquired. Two years after a PE firm sold a practice, 44% of physicians were still there, against 60% in comparable practices.

blocks.text: Retention bonuses buy time, not loyalty

runs.t: In Towers Watson's 2014 global study, 68% of acquirers kept more than 80% of retention agreement signers through the retention period. One year after it ended, only 43% still did. Retention periods are also getting shorter: WTW's 2024 study puts the median at 13 to 18 months. A bonus keeps people until the bonus pays. It does not tell you who wanted to stay.

blocks.text: Longer holds raise the stakes

items.label: unsold PE-backed companies worth about $3.8 trillion (Bain, 2026)

of portfolio companies with succession planning (AlixPartners)

runs.t: Bain's 2026 Global Private Equity Report counts about 32,000 unsold portfolio companies worth about $3.8 trillion, with average holds at exit of about seven years. With multiples flat, value has to come from growth and operations. As AlixPartners and Heidrick & Struggles put it, longer holds mean "more time during which value must be created not through financing but operationally." Operations run on people.

blocks.text: What industry leaders are saying

blocks.title: “Too many private equity firms are still reacting to leadership crises instead of preventing or anticipating them.”
lines: Ted Bililies, PhD, Global Leader of Transformative Leadership, AlixPartners. 11th Annual PE Leadership Survey, March 2026.

blocks.title: “The private-equity model works best when investors and management teams are tightly aligned around how value will be created.”
lines: Madalyn Miller, Partner and Managing Director, AlixPartners. March 2026.

blocks.title: “We took the quit rate from almost 50% to 15%. That's transformational in terms of a culture.”
lines: Pete Stavros, Co-head of Global Private Equity, KKR, on a portfolio company's broad-based ownership program. ImpactAlpha, May 2025.

blocks.text: Our assessment: why key people leave after a deal

runs.t: Most firms treat talent as a CEO question. In our experience the deal is won or lost one layer down: the regional leaders, top sellers, plant managers and clinicians who run the business every day. These are the six forces we look for first.
1. Uncertainty starts before close.
The best people are the first to hear rumors and the first to get calls. Silence during diligence and signing is when they start looking.
2. The welcome is generic.
New owners send the same message to everyone. Nobody has a prioritized list of who matters most and what it would take to keep each of them.
3. Roles change without a conversation.
Bigger spans, new reporting lines and new metrics land on key people with little explanation of why.
4. The equity story is not their story.
Management equity reaches the top team. The layer below often sees more work, more targets and no share in the upside.
5. Integration lands on the same few people.
Add-ons, system changes and cost programs are carried by a handful of capable operators. They burn out first.
6. Bonuses create cliffs.
Retention payments end on a date. Without a reason to stay beyond the money, the cliff becomes an exit date.

blocks.text: What we saw inside a Fortune 10 company

runs.t: Before founding EIP, I spent 20 years in operations at a Fortune 10 company, through several large acquisitions and restructurings.

When we acquired a large number of stores from another retailer, the announcement came with fanfare and new signs. But for many of the people we inherited, pay and benefits were going to get worse, and they knew it. We treated retention as one generic welcome effort. We had no prioritized list of who to keep, and no plan for what it would take to keep each of them. Some of that talent was strong, and some had worked for us before. We lost good people we should not have lost.

In a later restructuring, consultants were brought in to evaluate our people. Managers fed in talent reviews, and the work became a large reduction in force. Leaders were given more stores and more span of control with no increase in pay, and avoidable mistakes followed. A partner who had listened to the field would have avoided a lot of pain.
The lesson:
in a deal, look at your talent person by person. How much impact does each key person have, and what would it take to keep them? Use a personalized plan, not a pizza party and new signs.

We have also seen the other side. In a region I led, turnover among our 24 district leaders went from about four quits a year to one once we fixed the store-level turnover that was burning them out. In energy, we built a Flight Risk Score for an oil and gas company. The person at the top of the anonymized list, scored 82, had resigned the week before.

With the HR data available in diligence, we can show where retention risk sits in the roles your thesis depends on.
2. Retention Snapshot for a portfolio company, by invitation.

Send one spreadsheet for one to three job titles that share a pay band, a location and the same kind of work, such as regional or site leaders, for a small group. Names are replaced with codes. See first Flight Risk Score and Turn Tax numbers in about 7 days.
3. 30-day diagnostic.
Who is at risk, what it costs, and why, through the data and Honest Read™ interviews with the people who carry the business.
4. The Council decides what to fix.
Our Council of current and former executives and operators reviews the findings and chooses the best-fit fixes before anything is recommended.
5. We stay through the hold.
Council View tracks the numbers that predict departure every month, so your board sees retention risk next to every other operating metric.
One engagement can run across several portfolio companies, so an operating partner sees talent risk across the fund in one view.

blocks.text: Your first 100 days

rows: Name the 20 to 50 people the value-creation plan cannot lose. Not by title. By impact.
Talk to each of them personally. Why they matter, what will change, what will not, and what happens next.
Score flight risk across those roles and the layer below. Ask your longest-tenured operators: if you had no money but could fix one thing, what would it be?
Build a personal retention plan for every critical person in Intervention needed or Critical. Pay, role, career and workload, not just a bonus.
Put retention risk on the monthly board dashboard, next to EBITDA and the value-creation plan.

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: Operating partner: Pick one portfolio company. Ask its CEO to name the ten people the plan cannot lose, and when each last had a real career conversation.
Deal partner: On your next deal, ask for 24 months of departures below the C-suite in diligence. The pattern tells you more than the org chart.
Human capital partner: List retention bonus end dates across the portfolio for the next 12 months. Each one is a possible exit date.
Portfolio CEO: Find the five people carrying the most integration work. Ask what would make it sustainable, and act on one answer.
Portfolio CFO: Add up recruiting fees, interim leaders and retention bonuses last year. Compare it with the Turn Tax for your key roles.

blocks.text: Start with a conversation

runs.t: If you lead a PE firm or a portfolio company and want to know who is at risk, what it is costing you and what to fix first, start with a Retention Snapshot, by invitation. One spreadsheet, one to three titles, a small group, and first numbers in about 7 days.
